title: Project 3 - Walter_Vandenborne
text: Project 3 Project 3 serves as the clinical research project for this Center application, complementing preclinical therapeutic development in Projects 1 & 2. Building on our expertise in noninvasive magnetic resonance (MR) biomarker development, we determine the contemporary natural history of gene therapy treated patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and in a rare form of limb girdle muscular dystrophy, sarcoglycanopathy (LGMDR3/R5). Our central hypothesis is that quantitative MR can be used as a biomarker for early skeletal and cardiac muscle disease progression and inflammation, to monitor the impact of AAV based therapies. Micro-dystrophin (µDys) gene therapy has emerged as a promising treatment strategy with recent FDA approval changing the landscape in DMD. However, the truncated nature of the µDys protein and the need for high concentrations of current AAVs may limit therapeutic efficacy and present some unique challenges. Therefore, in Aim 1 we will determine the disease trajectory of individuals with DMD treated with a clinically approved µDys-AAV and evaluate the impact on cardiac muscle. In Aim 2, we will extend our biomarker work to LGMDR3/R5, an underserved patient population in therapeutic development. We will use a combination of MR biomarkers and serum/urine biomarkers to characterize the natural history of disease progression and help identify therapeutic targets and novel biomarkers for future AAV clinical trials in this population. Finally, in Aim 3, we will validate MR parametric mapping of the myocardium to detect cardiac remodeling, inflammation, and any reaction to a large dose of AAV in a large rodent model of DMD, with the goal of implementing this approach in young children undergoing gene therapy.

title: INPP5E Signaling and Treatment in Rheumatoid Arthritis
text:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a serious autoimmune and inflammatory disease affecting 1% of the
world's population. The proposed project aims to understand how INPP5E influences RA
pathogenesis and test a new treatment using novel targeted lipid nanoparticles to deliver INPP5E
mRNA in RA mouse models. We expect that this study will bring novel insights into the mechanism
of RA pathogenesis and provide a new mRNA therapy for RA and other inflammatory diseases.

title: Multimodal imaging biomarkers of cognitive control network deficits in youths with disruptive behavior
text:
Disruptive behavior disorders affect over 113 million children worldwide—making it a public health concern—
whereby approximately 50% of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have co-occurring disruptive
behavior that leads to greater impairment and long-term, intensive clinical interventions; however, no study has
examined brain biomarkers of disruptive behavior in children with and without ASD. The proposed study will be
the first to leverage connectomics, large-scale open science imaging data, and predictive modeling to
investigate novel, transdiagnostic biomarkers of disruptive behavior disorders in children with and without ASD.
Large multisite neuroimaging data affords unprecedented opportunities to close the gap between basic and
translational neuroscience, and to establish biomarkers that could advance development of new, targeted
interventions to optimize clinical outcomes.

title: Dissecting the Sox2-orchestrated transcriptional network that governs immune resistance in tumor initiating cells
text:
Cancer immunotherapy resistance in squamous cell carcinomas is found to be orchestrated by a
special group of tumor-initiating cells. This project aims to uncover novel mechanisms activated by
Sox2 to reprogram the immune suppressive microenvironment and intrinsic resistance of tumor-
initiating cells. The ultimate goal of this project is to leverage the findings from this study for more
effective immunotherapies that can overcome cancer recurrence.

title: A Dynamic and Three-Dimensional Human Model of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome to Probe Compromised Cardiomyocyte Proliferation
text:
Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is a severe type of congenital heart defects with poorly understood origins, partly
due to the lack of accessible biological models that can imitate key features of the disease. This proposal aims
to address these needs by developing a useful 3D bioprinted platform with disease-specific cells and applying it
as a laboratory model to better understand the progression of hypoplastic left heart syndrome in humans.
Information gathered from this study will, therefore, advance our overall comprehension of abnormal cardiac
development which could lead to new targets for preventative and therapeutic strategies.

title: The utility of cyclooxygenase-1 PET imaging as a novel neuroinflammatory biomarker for Alzheimer's disease
text:
The proposed research plan is relevant to public health because the project focuses on developing a
neuroinflammation-specific imaging biomarker for optimized therapeutic trials in Alzheimer’s disease. Once such
biomarker has been developed and used to improve the efficiency of therapeutic trials, this research has the
potential to facilitate the discovery of new therapies for Alzheimer’s disease. The proposed research is also
relevant to the part of the NIA’s mission that pertains to improving the health and well-being of older adults,
because prevention or treatment of Alzheimer’s disease is one of the most urgent healthcare needs of the
growing older adult population.

title: Targeting T Cell Senescence and Dysfunction for Anti-tumor Immunity
text:
The proposed studies address the important issue of immune suppression and dysfunction of tumor-reactive
T cells mediated by human regulatory T cells that is a major barrier for successful anti-tumor immunity and
immunotherapy. The proposed research has relevance to public health, because it seeks to dissect a novel
suppressive mechanism and then to develop critical strategies that control immune suppression mediated by
human regulatory T cells. Thus, the findings are ultimately expected to be applicable to improve the
treatments against human cancer and immune-related diseases as well.

title: Hyperspectral chemical imaging via sum-frequency generation microscopic holography
text:
Fast 3D imaging techniques are important for biomedical research and clinical diagnostics. This project seeks to 
develop a new nonlinear digital microscopic holography approach that can reveal chemical signatures and 
structural dynamics of biological specimens with unprecedented speeds. This transformational tool may provide 
deep insight into open questions and enable discoveries of disease mechanisms and new treatment paradigms.

title: Advanced culture and recording system for long-term electrophysiological profiling in human brain organoids
text:
Human “brain organoid” systems, cell culture models of human brain development derived from pluripotent
stem cells, are important for disease studies and drug testing in human brain cells and circuits. This project
will develop a novel electrophysiology system and critical components that, for the first time, will enable the
study of how changes in the cells and molecules within organoids affect the functional properties of their
neurons and circuits across timescales from milliseconds to weeks. This opens important new areas in basic
neuroscience and translational research.

title: Developing Woodchucks Susceptible to Hepatitis B Virus Infection by Modifying the Virus or Host
text:
Chronic infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) presents a global public health burden affecting 296 million
individuals worldwide, who are at high risk of developing severe liver diseases, including cirrhosis and
hepatocellular carcinoma, and will die without therapeutic intervention or liver transplantation. Our proposed
research seeks to render woodchucks susceptible to HBV infection by modifying either the virus or host. Our
project will provide a much-needed animal model for developing new, curative HBV-specific drugs for the
treatment of patients.

title: Endocrine-mediated pubertal brain network development: Bridging datasets with machine learning
text:
Puberty is a critical period for neuroendocrine development characterized by substantial neuroplasticity and
changing sex hormone levels, which are poorly understood in humans. Innovative analytic strategies are needed
for integrating data from multiple approaches (i.e., large- and small-scale datasets with sparse and dense
longitudinal sampling) to better characterize the contributions of long-term pubertal changes, and more short-
term monthly variability in hormones as it pertains to structure and function of the developing brain. The proposed
study will apply machine learning to assess hormone-related brain structure and functional connectivity, the roles
of sex hormones in microstructure-function coupling across the brain, and the impact of hormone variability and
sampling design on identified neuroendocrine phenomena.

title: Allosteric mechanisms in nucleic acid transactions by ligand-activated protein rings
text:
This project aims to elucidate the mechanisms by which ligand binding, nucleotide hydrolysis, and product
release are coupled to protein-mediated nucleic acid transformations. Understanding these processes in
homo-oligomeric ring-forming proteins will advance our knowledge of cellular functions such as mRNA
transcription regulation and DNA replication. This research may benefit human health by improving treatments
for diseases like cancer, viral infections, and antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

title: An Automated Multimodal, Multiscale Algorithm for Cervical Cancer Screening in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
text:
Cervical cancer is a life-threatening disease that is associated with microscopic and macroscopic changes in the
cervix, such as the development of lesions, and disproportionately affects low- and middle- income countries. A
major barrier in implementing and sustaining screening programs for cervical cancer in low-resource countries
is the lack of trained clinicians. This proposal will develop and evaluate a novel multimodal, multiscale deep
learning algorithm workflow that integrates microscopic and macroscopic features from cervical images to
automatically arrive at a diagnostic result, which could improve access to cervical cancer screening and
significantly decrease mortality due to the disease.

title: Pathogen Transmission Dynamics among Wildlife and Human Settlements in Rural Western Uganda
text:
This project will strengthen public health preparedness by improving the surveillance, detection, and characterization of pathogens at a globally important zoonotic spillover hotspot. 
Accurate identification of pathogen strains and transmission routes will improve understanding of how zoonotic diseases emerge, adapt and spread. Through integrated surveillance, genomic analyses, and predictive modeling, this project will generate knowledge directly relevant to protecting American health and interests by strengthening early detection, outbreak preparedness, risk assessment, and prevention strategies for emerging infectious diseases. Because pathogens that emerge abroad can rapidly spread through international travel and trade, identifying transmission pathways and factors that facilitate spillover will enhance genomic surveillance, inform public health interventions, and improve preparedness for future epidemic and pandemic threats to the United States and globally.

title: Stem cell regulation during development and whole-body regeneration
text:
This project is relevant to public health because it will identify molecular and cellular
mechanisms for how pluripotent stem cells can be established in embryos, retained into
adulthood, and then regulated for the formation of differentiated cell types in the context of a
whole animal. An understanding of these mechanisms is essential for progress in human
regenerative medicine and therefore relates to the NIH’s mission to acquire fundamental
knowledge about living systems that can be applied to human biology to reduce disability.

title: PREDICTIVE DRUG TESTING IN ORGANOID MODELS
text: High-throughput screening (HTS) of approved and investigational agents in organoid models established from patient-derived tumor tissues. These studies will assist NCI in identifying drug responsive tumors and enable the active investigation of the underlying mechanism(s) of action, predictive biomarkers of response and/or resistance to agents, and the effects of genetic alterations on drug efficacy.

title: Fibril-Targeting Nanobodies for Restoring Mitochondrial Stress and Cardiac Function in ATTR-CM
text:
Current therapies for transthyretin amyloidosis cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) fail to reverse disease progression,
leaving patients without effective options to restore cardiac function. This project aims to develop targeted
nanobody-based therapies while leveraging advanced human cardiac organoid models to uncover the molecular
mechanisms of mitochondrial and calcium dysregulation caused by amyloid fibril deposition. By addressing both
the therapeutic and mechanistic gaps, this research will significantly advance our understanding of ATTR-CM
and catalyze the development of transformative treatments.

title: Early to Late Events in Colorectal Neoplasia: Basic Biology to Clinical Implementation
text:
At least 85% of colorectal cancer (CRC), the 2nd most frequent cause of cancer deaths worldwide, is due to
microsatellite stable (MSS) CRC, which does not respond to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), in contrast to
microsatellite unstable (MSI-H), in which durable remissions are achieved with ICB. By combing single-cell RNA-
sequencing (scRNA-seq), regional whole exome sequencing (WES), spatial transcriptomics (ST) and MxIF to
enumerate consensus cell states and to project tumor programs and microenvironmental features onto
progression pseudotime, we have identified an immune-exclusion IEX score in MSS CRC that consists of DDR1,
TGFBi and DPEP1, which are markedly upregulated in plasma-derived small extracellullar vesicles (sEVs) and
supermeres of CRC patients compared to healthy controls, and for which inhibitors are developed or being
developed. In this R35 renewal, we propose to explore mechanisms by which these proteins promote
tumorigenesis, develop them as liquid biomarkers, and introduce novel strategies to introduce inhibitors to them
in the clinic.

title: The role of KCNS3 in Dopaminergic Neuron Pacemaking and Parkinson's Disease
text:
Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a debilitating neurodegenerative movement disorder caused by a loss of
dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. This proposal will study a high-risk PD gene,
KCNS3, which encodes a voltage-gated K+ channel subunit and how it impacts the membrane properties
and vulnerability of these dopaminergic neurons. Knowledge gained from these experiments will provide
new insights into mechanisms increasing the vulnerability substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons and hence
PD.

title: Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying defensosome biogenesis and release
text:
Our lab previously discovered an innate immune strategy wherein cells produce extracellular vesicles termed
defensosomes that neutralize bacterial toxins and viral pathogens. The proposed study will investigate the
molecular mechanisms by which the autophagy pathway and toll-like receptor signaling promote defensosome
biogenesis and release, thereby providing insights into the cellular pathways involved in host defense and
extracellular vesicle biology.
